promptText: According to Kent C. Dodds' "testing trophy" (as opposed to the classic testing pyramid), which layer should typically get the most testing effort for a frontend application, and why?
options: Integration tests, because rendering a component and interacting with it the way a user would gives the best confidence-per-effort ratio for UI that is mostly glue code
End-to-end tests, because only a real browser can ever prove the application works correctly
Unit tests of every individual function, because they are the fastest tests to run and should therefore dominate the suite
Static analysis alone, because TypeScript and ESLint make runtime tests unnecessary for a well-typed codebase
explanation: The testing trophy reshapes the pyramid for frontend work: a small base of unit tests, a large middle layer of integration tests (render a component/small tree and interact with it like a user, mocking only true boundaries like the network), and a thin top layer of E2E -- because integration tests give the best confidence-per-effort for UI code that is mostly wiring between components and data.

promptText: A test needs to assert that an error message is NOT present after a form successfully submits. Which query should be used, and why?
options: queryByText, because it returns null instead of throwing when there is no match, which is the only way to cleanly assert an element's absence
getByText, because it always returns the first matching element or undefined if none exists
findByText, because it is the only query that supports negative assertions with .not
getAllByText, because asserting absence requires checking that the returned array has more than zero elements
explanation: getBy* throws an error when no match is found, which makes it the wrong tool for asserting something is absent -- the test would error instead of cleanly failing or passing. queryBy* returns null on no match, so `expect(screen.queryByText(...)).not.toBeInTheDocument()` is the idiomatic way to assert absence.

promptText: Why does React Testing Library's documentation recommend `getByRole` over `getByTestId` as the default way to find elements?
options: getByRole queries the DOM the way assistive technology does, by role and accessible name, so a passing test is also evidence the element is reachable by screen-reader users; getByTestId has no user-facing meaning at all
getByTestId is deprecated and will be removed in a future version of Testing Library
getByRole runs faster than getByTestId because it does not need to traverse the DOM tree
getByTestId only works with class components, while getByRole works with both class and function components
explanation: getByRole mirrors how screen readers and other assistive technology perceive the page (role + accessible name), so using it as the default query is a free, automatic accessibility check. getByTestId is an escape hatch reserved for elements with no meaningful role or text, since a data-testid attribute has no bearing on real user experience.

promptText: A test uses `fireEvent.click(disabledButton)` and the click handler fires anyway, even though the button has the `disabled` attribute. The same test rewritten with `userEvent.click(disabledButton)` correctly does nothing. What explains the difference?
options: fireEvent dispatches a single raw DOM event regardless of element state, while user-event simulates realistic browser behavior and will not click or type into a disabled element, matching what happens in a real browser
fireEvent is deprecated and no longer respects any HTML attributes at all
userEvent requires an explicit disabled prop check in the test itself before it will skip the click
fireEvent and userEvent behave identically; the difference described must be a bug in the test setup
explanation: fireEvent just dispatches the named event directly, with no regard for whether a real browser would have allowed the interaction. user-event models a full, realistic user interaction and will not fire a click on a disabled element, which is exactly what a real browser does -- this is one of the concrete reasons user-event is the recommended default over fireEvent.

promptText: A test does nothing but call a function with no assertions at all: `test("covers add", () => { add(2, 3); });`. If Jest reports this line as covered, what does that actually prove?
options: Only that the code executed without throwing -- code coverage measures which lines ran, not whether any assertion verified the result was correct
That add(2, 3) returns the correct value, since Jest automatically checks the return value of any function called inside a test
That the function has zero bugs, since 100% line coverage is mathematically equivalent to full correctness
Nothing, because Jest requires at least one expect() call per test or it will fail to report coverage at all
explanation: Coverage tools like Istanbul only track which lines/branches/functions actually executed during the test run. A test with no expect() can still mark every executed line as 'covered' while verifying nothing -- coverage measures execution, not correctness, which is why chasing a coverage percentage is not the same as chasing real confidence.

promptText: What is the main advantage of using MSW (Mock Service Worker) to test a component that fetches data, compared to directly stubbing `global.fetch = jest.fn()`?
options: MSW intercepts requests at the network layer, so the component's real fetching code (fetch, axios, React Query, etc.) runs completely unchanged and unexercised code paths in the request/response handling get tested too
MSW is faster than stubbing fetch because it runs entirely inside the V8 engine with no interception overhead
Stubbing fetch directly is impossible in Jest, so MSW is the only way to test any component that makes a network request
MSW automatically generates test assertions based on the shape of the API response, removing the need to write expect() calls
explanation: Directly mocking fetch requires hand-building Response-shaped objects and couples the test to the specific transport library used; MSW intercepts at the network layer below your code, so the actual request-building and response-parsing logic in the component runs for real and gets exercised by the test, rather than being bypassed entirely.

promptText: An element has both visible text content "Edit" and `aria-labelledby="section-title"` pointing at an `<h2>` that reads "Billing address". Which accessible name would `getByRole('button', { name: ... })` need to match?
options: "Billing address", because aria-labelledby overrides the element's own text content in the accessible-name computation, even though "Edit" is what a sighted user sees
"Edit", because an element's own text content always takes priority over any ARIA attribute
Both "Edit" and "Billing address" simultaneously, since Testing Library concatenates all possible name sources
Neither, because an element cannot have both visible text and an aria-labelledby attribute at the same time
explanation: The accessible-name computation resolves aria-labelledby first, before aria-label, a native label, or the element's own text content. So even though a sighted user sees 'Edit', the computed accessible name -- and what getByRole's name option must match -- is 'Billing address', the referenced heading's text.

promptText: A table renders one row per user, and each row has its own "Delete" button with identical accessible names. `screen.getByRole('button', { name: /delete/i })` throws because it matches multiple elements. What is the recommended fix, and why is it better than adding a unique `data-testid` to each button?
options: Scope the query with within(), first finding the specific row (e.g. by its accessible name) and then querying for the Delete button inside that row -- this keeps the query behavior-focused instead of reintroducing implementation-coupled test-only attributes
Add a unique data-testid to each row's button, since within() cannot be used when multiple elements share the same role and name
Switch to container.querySelectorAll and manually index into the array, since Testing Library has no way to disambiguate identical roles
Rename the buttons in the component so no two rows ever share the same visible text, even if that changes the intended UI copy
explanation: within(element) scopes the same query functions to a specific subtree, so you can find the target row first (by its own accessible name) and then query for the Delete button only within that row -- resolving the ambiguity structurally while still using accessible, behavior-focused queries rather than falling back to test-only attributes or brittle indexing.

promptText: A team is deciding between Jest and Vitest for a new project. What is the most accurate guidance for making that choice today?
options: Choose based on the build toolchain: Vitest is the natural fit for a Vite-based app since it reuses Vite's transform pipeline and needs no separate Babel/ts-jest config, while Jest remains a fine choice for an established webpack/Next.js setup
Always choose Vitest, since Jest has been fully deprecated and is no longer maintained by the JavaScript community
Always choose Jest, since Vitest cannot run React Testing Library tests or any Jest-compatible matchers
The choice is irrelevant because Vitest and Jest use completely incompatible test syntax, requiring a full rewrite either way
explanation: Vitest was designed as a near drop-in replacement for Jest's API (describe/it/expect, similar mocking with vi instead of jest) and is fastest specifically when it can share a Vite project's existing transform pipeline. Jest remains the well-supported default for Next.js/webpack codebases with an established setup -- the decision is mostly dictated by toolchain fit, not by one tool being categorically better.

promptText: A large component's snapshot test (`expect(container).toMatchSnapshot()`) fails on nearly every PR that touches the component, and the team has developed a habit of running `jest -u` to accept the new snapshot without reading the diff. What is the core problem this illustrates?
options: The snapshot test has stopped providing real protection -- since updates are accepted without review, it no longer verifies the output is correct, only that someone pressed a key to accept whatever the code currently produces
Snapshot tests are fundamentally broken in Jest and should never be used under any circumstances
The problem is purely a tooling bug that would be fixed by switching to inline snapshots instead of file-based ones
This is expected and healthy behavior, since accepting a new snapshot is equivalent to a human confirming the change is correct
explanation: A large snapshot on a frequently-changed component produces noisy diffs on every legitimate change, and because updating is a single keystroke, teams reflexively accept without reviewing -- at that point the test rubber-stamps whatever the code currently does and provides no real regression protection. The fix is smaller, more focused snapshots (or inline snapshots) and explicit behavioral assertions for anything that actually matters.

promptText: When testing a component connected to a Redux store, why is creating a real store with `configureStore({ reducer, preloadedState })` generally preferred over mocking `useSelector` and `useDispatch` directly?
options: A real store exercises the actual reducers and selectors, so the test verifies real state-derivation logic; mocking the hooks only proves the component calls dispatch with an expected shape, never that the reducer produces correct resulting state
Mocking useSelector and useDispatch is not technically possible in Jest, so a real store is the only working option
Real stores run significantly faster in tests than mocked selectors, which is the primary reason to prefer them
A real store is required because React Testing Library refuses to render any component that imports react-redux
explanation: Mocking useSelector/useDispatch isolates the component from its actual state logic, so the test can pass even if the real reducer has a bug. A real store with preloadedState lets the actual reducer and selector code run, giving genuine confidence in the component-to-store wiring rather than just confirming the component called dispatch with an expected argument shape.

promptText: A test file calls `jest.mock('../api/userClient', () => ({ getUser: jest.fn()... }))` at the top, referencing an outer variable named `fakeUser` inside the factory, and gets an out-of-scope reference error. What is the underlying cause?
options: jest.mock calls are hoisted by Jest to the top of the file, above all imports and variable declarations, so the factory cannot reference an out-of-scope variable unless its name is prefixed with 'mock'
jest.mock factories can never reference any variable under any circumstances, including variables prefixed with 'mock'
The error means the module path is misspelled, since hoisting has nothing to do with variable scoping
jest.mock only supports arrow functions as factories, and the error indicates a regular function was used instead
explanation: Jest hoists jest.mock calls above imports so the mock is in place before the real module is ever required. This means a factory referencing an outer-scope variable will fail unless Jest specifically allows it -- which it does only for variable names prefixed with 'mock', a naming convention Jest's babel transform specifically recognizes as safe to hoist alongside the mock call.

promptText:
A test for a `ShopPage` component does `jest.mock('./CartSummary', () => () =>
Mocked Summary
)` and then asserts the mocked text appears. A teammate later introduces a real bug in `CartSummary`'s total-calculation logic. What happens to this test, and what does that reveal?
options: The test still passes, because CartSummary's real implementation never runs -- this reveals the test was never actually exercising the page-to-CartSummary wiring or CartSummary's own logic, only proving the mock renders what it was told to render
The test fails immediately, because Jest automatically detects when a mocked component's real implementation has a bug
The test fails only if the bug also affects the ShopPage component's own code, never if it's isolated to CartSummary
The test's outcome is unrelated to mocking and depends entirely on whether CartSummary is a class or function component
explanation: Mocking your own child component means its real implementation never executes during the test, so a bug introduced inside CartSummary's actual logic has no way to be caught by this test. The diagnostic technique of deliberately breaking real code and checking whether a suspect test still passes is exactly how this kind of over-mocking is caught -- if it still passes, the mock replaced the very thing the test was supposed to verify.

promptText: A test reads: `const getUser = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ name: "Ada" }); const result = getUser(); expect(result).resolves.toEqual({ name: "Ada" });`. Why is this assertion considered close to worthless despite passing?
options: It is tautological -- it only verifies that the mock returns the exact value it was explicitly configured to return, so it can never fail regardless of whether any real application code has a bug
It is worthless because resolves.toEqual is not a valid Jest matcher and the test would actually throw a syntax error
It is worthless only because the mock function is unnamed; naming it 'mockGetUser' would fix the underlying issue
It correctly and meaningfully tests the getUser function's real behavior and should be considered a good test
explanation: This assertion re-confirms the mock's own configured return value rather than testing anything about how application code uses that value -- it is impossible for this specific assertion to fail regardless of what bugs exist elsewhere. The useful version instead renders the real component consuming the mocked dependency and asserts on the resulting user-visible behavior, so a bug in how the component handles the resolved data would actually cause a failure.

promptText: A test suite has `const cart = createCart();` declared once at module scope (outside any beforeEach), used and mutated by multiple tests in the file. One test passes when run in isolation (`jest cart.test.js -t "starts empty"`) but fails when the full file runs together. What is the most precise diagnosis?
options: Shared mutable state: an earlier test in the same file mutated the module-level cart object, and because it was never reset before the next test ran, that leftover state leaked into a later test that assumed a fresh cart
The test framework has a bug that only manifests when more than one test exists in the same file
jsdom resets all module-level variables between individual test() blocks, so the failure must be caused by an unrelated async timing issue
Jest always runs tests in a random order by default, which is the only possible explanation for order-dependent failures
explanation: A module-level object created once and mutated by multiple tests without being reset is the classic shared-mutable-state bug -- the telltale symptom is exactly 'passes alone, fails as part of the full suite (or in a different order)', because an earlier test's mutations to the shared object are still present when a later test runs. The fix is to create a fresh cart inside beforeEach so every test starts from known, isolated state.
